title: Runtime hotpatch and quick redeploy playbook
author: Lina Zhang
content:
Summary

This playbook captures step-by-step guidance for applying small, targeted hotpatches to the serving runtime (kernel or scheduling components) and for performing a fast emergency redeploy when a hotpatch is not possible or has failed. It targets oncall engineers and runtime SREs who must restore service within the next 15–60 minutes while preserving customer SLOs and minimizing blast radius.

When to use this playbook

- Critical kernel or scheduler bug causing elevated 99th-percentile latency or hard errors (5xx) for >1 minute and automatic mitigations have not restored SLOs.
- Memory corruption or a known safe patch exists that can be applied without a full image build.
- Emergency patch path is documented in the kernel safety-net and approved by the runtime owner.
- If the issue is a broader configuration, refer to the deployment circuit-breakers playbook instead.

Owners and escalation

- Primary: runtime-oncall (pager duty) — first responder.
- Secondary: runtime-sre (pager) — 10 minutes escalation if unresolved.
- Tertiary:serving-runtime-eng (email/Slack) — for cross-team rollout coordination.

Required checks before hotpatching (preflight)

1) Confirm actual customer impact:
   - Check per-route 99th latency spikes and 5xx rate in the last 5 minutes.
   - Verify error budgets: if < 10% remaining for the hour, proceed with caution.

2) Validate trace and kernel signal presence:
   - Look up last 100 traces that hit the failing path (trace tag: runtime.kernel.failure=true).
   - Confirm root cause candidate aligns with a supported hotpatch (see Acceptable Hotpatch Types table below).

3) Confirm rollback path and canary target nodes are available:
   - Identify a canary cohort of 5–10% of nodes in the affected pool (minimum 3 nodes).
   - Ensure at least one warm spare pool is ready for immediate slot migration.

Acceptable Hotpatch Types (short table)

| Hotpatch Type | Allowed when | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| JIT config tweak (no binary change) | Fixes runtime flags or scheduler thresholds | Low |
| Lua/JS actuator script swap | Script corrects route matching / backoff | Low–medium |
| Binary function-level hotfix (approved diff) | Small critical logic change with signed patch | Medium |
| Kernel microservice restart with staged image | When binary replacement is required but can be canaried | Medium–high |

Note: Full binary rebuilds that change kernel ABI are NOT eligible for hotpatch and require a standard canary image rollout.

Hotpatch procedure (fast path) — target time 15–25 minutes

1) Announce intent (1 minute)
   - Post to #runtime-incidents with: incident id, short description, target nodes, and expected time window.

2) Quiesce auxiliary load (2 minutes)
   - Use the admission controller to shift non-critical burst traffic: 
     redwoodctl route-weight --scope affected --weight 0.1 --duration 5m
   - Enable temporary cache bypass for debug traces: 
     redwoodctl debug cache-bypass --routes debug-* --on

3) Apply the hotpatch to canary cohort (3–5 minutes)
   - For config/script changes: push via the config service: 
     curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/v1/hotpatch -d '{"patch":"<base64>"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
   - For signed binary microfix: use the runtime hotpatch signer: 
     redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --patch-file /tmp/patch.bin --signature /tmp/patch.sig
   - Confirm deployment status: 
     redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort canary --wait 60s

4) Observe telemetry for 10 minutes (minimum)
   - Dashboards to watch: per-node 99th latency, per-route 5xx rate, kernel-exception-rate.
   - Run smoke query: 
     curl -sS https://svc-internal/health-check -H 'x-test-trace: hotpatch-canary' | jq .status

5) If stable -> progressive expand (10–20 minutes)
   - Expand cohort in steps: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%, with 5–10 minute observation windows between steps.
   - Use automated rollout: 
     redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval 5m --steps 10,30,60,100 --cohort affected

Emergency redeploy procedure (when hotpatch fails or not allowed) — target time 30–60 minutes

1) Abort any in-flight hotpatch and mark canary as failed:
   - redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --abort --reason "hotpatch failed"

2) Prepare a fast redeploy image (prebuilt emergency image recommended)
   - If a prebuilt emergency image exists, tag it as emergency: 
     redwoodctl image tag --image-id img-2026-11-09-emergency --tag emergency-<incident-id>
   - If not, build minimal image with the exact production ABI and only the required fix. Use the fast-build profile: 
     ./build-image --profile fast --include runtime:hotfix-module --tag emergency-<incident-id>

3) Canary redeploy to the canary cohort (5–10 minutes)
   - Deploy the emergency image to the canary cohort: 
     redwoodctl deploy --image emergency-<incident-id> --cohort canary --max-concurrency 3
   - Attach observability hooks: trace-sampling=100%, metric-enrichment=hotpatch-incident.<id>

4) Automated smoke and runbook checks (10–15 minutes)
   - Run the smoke suite against the canary: 
     redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort canary --tests core-latency,kv-consistency,session-stability --timeout 600s
   - Verify no increase in memory RSS, no new 5xx, and no kernel panics.

5) Expand or rollback (progressive)
   - Follow the same progressive expansion steps as the hotpatch procedure.
   - If at any point the 99th latency or 5xx rates regress above pre-incident thresholds, trigger rollback immediately.

Rollback and containment

- To rollback a hotpatch to the previous known-good state: 
  redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort affected --rollback-to stable-<timestamp> --force-checks
- To rollback a redeploy: 
  redwoodctl deploy --image stable-image-<timestamp> --cohort affected --force
- Containment steps if rollback is not possible quickly: 
  1) Shift traffic away from affected pool using route weights.
  2) Attach fallback routing: 
     redwoodctl routing fallback --policy model-variant --target variant-stable --duration 30m

Telemetry and post-incident tasks

- During the operation ensure the following metrics are captured at 10s granularity for at least 30 minutes: per-node cpu/gpu utilization, per-node memory RSS, kernel-exception-rate, per-route 99p latency, per-route 5xx rate, kvcache-hitratio.
- Create an incident bridge note with timeline and include command transcripts.
- Postmortem: owner is runtime-sre; draft within 72 hours; public summary to go-to-market within 7 days if customer-facing.

Command reference (common commands)

- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --patch-file <file> --signature <sig>
- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --abort --reason <text>
- redwoodctl deploy --image <image-tag> --cohort <cohort> --max-concurrency <n>
- redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval <min> --steps <csv> --cohort <cohort>
- redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort <cohort> --tests <list> --timeout <s>
- redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort <cohort> --wait <s>

Safety thresholds (must abort and rollback if any triggered)

- Per-route 5xx rate increases by >200% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Per-route 99p latency increases by >50% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Any kernel panic or OOM observed on >1% of nodes in cohort.

Configuration snippets and examples

- Example emergency rollout policy (YAML):

  apiVersion: redwood/v1
  kind: RolloutPolicy
  metadata:
    name: emergency-fast-expansion
  spec:
    strategy: progressive
    steps: [10, 30, 60, 100]
    intervalMinutes: 5
    maxConcurrency: 5
    safetyChecks:
      - metric: kernel-panic-count
        threshold: 1
        windowSeconds: 60

- Example smoke test list (JSON array):

  ["core-latency","kv-consistency","session-stability","model-fidelity-basic"]

Post-incident hygiene checklist

1) Record the exact patch artifact and commit hash used.
2) Create a test matrix entry that reproduces the failure in the sandbox.
3) Schedule a controlled rebuild and standard canary for the patch (no emergency tags) within 72 hours.
4) Update the kernel hotpatch whitelist if the hotpatch type will be reused.
5) Update runbook: add any missing steps or commands discovered during the incident.

Appendices

A. Quick diagnostics commands
- tail -n 200 /var/log/runtime/kernel.log | grep -i panic
- redwoodctl metrics query "avg(99p_latency) by route" --from -10m
- redwoodctl traces query --tag runtime.kernel.failure --limit 100

B. Canary cohort sizing guidance
- For small pools (< 100 nodes) use minimum 3-node canary.
- For large pools (> 1000 nodes) prefer 5–10% but cap canary at 200 nodes.

C. Links and references
- Kernel safety and rollback playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-safety-net-and-rollback-playbook-2027
- Deployment circuit breakers: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- Canary matrix and validation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

If you are the oncall taking this action: add your name to the incident timeline and ping runtime-sre for audit and postmortem ownership.
